question: Whether WinINet's capture records an exchange made through WinINet asynchronously as it records one made synchronously - every part exact, numbered and flagged, in the same buffers - and which of the client's threads raises each record.
answer: As a synchronous one's: every part of every exchange was exact, numbered from 0 and flagged at its ends, sent bodies cut at 64,511 bytes and read bodies in the client's reads, nothing lost, every record the client process's. In either mode a record is raised on whichever of the process's threads finished the step it records: every head and every sent body's bytes on one of WinINet's own; a read's bytes on the thread that read them where they were waiting, and on one of WinINet's where the read waited for them; the empty buffer that ends a request body, raised after its response ended, and the one that ends a response, on the thread that read the response's end. A synchronous client's records split between the threads alike, so a record's thread is not the thread that made the request, in either mode.

capture.command: icat record --profile content --source etw/manifest/Microsoft-Windows-WinINet-Capture --mechanism http --pid <workload> --channel * --max-record-bytes 65536 --max-session-bytes 67108864 --inspection hex-text --duration 25, beside InterCat.TestWorkloads http-wininet --requests 64 --bytes 98304 --start-after 8 --async [--pace 5] [--concurrency 8 --chunked]; then icat exchanges --exchanges 10000 --decode, and each part of each exchange saved by icat content --part and matched by SHA-256

runs.run: async, paced, eight at once, chunked

ledger: fixtures/FX-HTTP-005/evidence/eight-at-once/buffers.csv: each buffer the probe captured of its 64 exchanges, in time order - its 100 ns readings after the first, event, exchange number, place, ends, length, the request its exchange's head named, and whether a thread that made a request raised it - never its bytes. A test groups it as a session's records are grouped.
note: Request 0's body is empty and raises no record; request 1's response is empty and is one buffer of no byte, which icat content says holds nothing to save. The parts are compared with the server's truth by length and SHA-256, a response body with what the client read; neither the truth nor this file holds a byte of them. A send pended in every asynchronous run; a read finished at once wherever its bytes were waiting, which the server's pacing made rarer.
